name: Supreme Court of India Landmark Precedents
description: Authoritative constitutional rulings of the Supreme Court of India defining fundamental rights, basic structure, and judicial review.

articles.number: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
articles.title: Basic Structure Doctrine & Limits on Amending Power
articles.text: Citation: (1973) 4 SCC 225. A historic 13-judge bench held that Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is wide, but not unlimited. Parliament cannot amend, alter, or destroy the 'Basic Structure' or essential constitutional framework (including democracy, republican form of government, secularism, separation of powers, and judicial review). Overruled Golaknath and preserved constitutional supremacy.

articles.number: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
articles.title: Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21 - Just, Fair, and Reasonable Law
articles.text: Citation: 1978 AIR 597. The Supreme Court revolutionized Article 21 by holding that 'procedure established by law' cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive; it must satisfy the test of being just, fair, and reasonable. Established the 'Golden Triangle'—holding that Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Freedoms), and 21 (Life and Liberty) are not isolated silos but are intimately interconnected. Natural justice and audi alteram partem are implicit in Article 21.

articles.number: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
articles.title: Fundamental Right to Privacy under Article 21
articles.text: Citation: (2017) 10 SCC 1. A unanimous 9-judge bench held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental and inalienable right intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. Privacy encompasses bodily integrity, personal autonomy, and informational privacy. Any state encroachment on privacy must satisfy legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.

articles.number: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
articles.title: Decriminalization of Consensual LGBTQ+ Relations & Constitutional Morality
articles.text: Citation: (2018) 1 SCC 791. A 5-judge constitution bench unanimously struck down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code to the extent it criminalized consensual same-sex acts between adults. Held that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates Article 14 (Equality), Article 15 (Non-discrimination on grounds of sex), and Article 21 (Dignity and Personal Autonomy). Courts must uphold 'Constitutional Morality' over popular or majoritarian morality.

articles.number: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
articles.title: Freedom of Speech Online & Striking down Section 66A IT Act
articles.text: Citation: (2015) 5 SCC 1. Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as unconstitutional for violating freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). The Court drew a clear distinction between 'discussion', 'advocacy', and 'incitement', ruling that mere advocacy or discussion of an unpopular cause cannot be penalized unless it reaches the threshold of clear and imminent incitement.

articles.title: Protection Against Workplace Sexual Harassment
articles.text: Citation: (1997) 6 SCC 241. In the absence of enacted domestic legislation, the Supreme Court laid down legally binding 'Vishaka Guidelines' under Article 32 and Article 141 to prevent sexual harassment of women at the workplace. Held that sexual harassment violates women's fundamental rights to equality (Articles 14 & 15), life and liberty (Article 21), and right to practice any profession (Article 19(1)(g)).

articles.number: Indira Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
articles.title: Mandal Case - 50% Ceiling on Reservations & Creamy Layer
articles.part: Judicial Precedent - Social Justice & Affirmative Action
articles.text: Citation: 1993 Supp (3) SCC 217. A 9-judge bench upheld 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) under Article 16(4), but established two crucial constitutional safeguards: (1) Total reservations must not exceed the 50% limit in ordinary circumstances to preserve efficiency and equality under Article 16(1); and (2) Advanced sections of backward classes ('Creamy Layer') must be excluded from affirmative action benefits.

articles.number: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
articles.title: Harmonious Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
articles.text: Citation: (1980) 3 SCC 625. Struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 inserted by the 42nd Amendment which sought to bar judicial review. Reaffirmed that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential feature of the Basic Structure. Fundamental Rights are the ends, and DPSP are the means; neither can be exalted over the other to destroy the constitutional fabric.

articles.number: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)
articles.title: Abolition of Instant Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-Biddat)
articles.text: Citation: (2017) 9 SCC 1. A 5-judge constitution bench by majority held instant Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-Biddat) to be unconstitutional and void. Held that unilateral, irrevocable divorce without reconciliation is manifestly arbitrary and violates Article 14. Practices that violate the dignity of women cannot claim protection under Article 25 (Freedom of Religion).

articles.number: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
articles.title: Federalism, Secularism, and Judicial Review of Article 356
articles.text: Citation: (1994) 3 SCC 1. A 9-judge bench curbed the arbitrary dismissal of state governments by the central executive under Article 356 (President's Rule). Ruled that the proclamation of President's Rule is subject to judicial review. Declared Secularism and Federalism to be integral parts of the Basic Structure. The floor test in the Legislative Assembly is the sole constitutional method to test the majority of a government.

articles.number: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)
articles.title: Freedom of the Press & Circulation
articles.text: Citation: 1950 AIR 124. Held that the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the freedom of propagation of ideas, which is ensured by the freedom of circulation. A government ban on the entry and circulation of a journal in a State is unconstitutional unless strictly justified under Article 19(2).

articles.number: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)
articles.title: Right to Livelihood is Inseparable from Right to Life
articles.text: Citation: (1985) 3 SCC 545. A 5-judge bench ruled that the Right to Livelihood is an integral part of the Right to Life under Article 21. If the right to livelihood were not treated as part of the constitutional right to life, the easiest way of depriving a person of his life would be to deprive him of his means of earning a living. State evictions require procedural fairness and natural justice.
